title: Peek-a-Boo Damselfly Wins Top Prize in Ecology Photo Contest
summary:
A tiny damselfly with a big personality has stolen the show in the 2026 BMC Ecology and Evolution and BMC Zoology image competition. The overall winning photo, taken by Sritam Kumar Sethy in a freshwater wetland in Odisha, India, shows an orange-tailed marsh dart damselfly (Ceriagrion cerinorubellum) peering through a hole in a leaf. Judge David Ferrier said, "It is hard not to smile at this beautifully composed and vivid image, in which the damselfly seems to display a remarkable sense of character and presence."

But the photo is more than just cute. Damselflies are critical predators in wetland ecosystems and serve as indicators of ecosystem health. Because they depend on both aquatic and terrestrial habitats, they are highly sensitive to pollution, habitat loss, and climate change. Editor Jennifer Harman noted that the image "highlights the importance of wetlands, which support a remarkable diversity of species yet are among the world's most threatened and rapidly disappearing habitats."

The competition, now in its fourth year, celebrates the beauty of life on Earth and the researchers working to protect it. Other winners include a striking shot of two students attaching a radio transmitter to a northern red-legged frog in Oregon at night—technology that helps scientists track animal movement and improve conservation. Another image captures the intense mating battle of giant Australian cuttlefish, whose skin pigmentation shifts dramatically as they compete for females. A photo of noisy friarbirds mobbing a brown goshawk in Australia illustrates a common anti-predator behavior, while a heartwarming image shows an olive ridley sea turtle hatchling being escorted to the sea by community members who protected its nest.

From drone surveys of the St. Lawrence Seaway to undergraduate research in the Everglades, these photos reveal the dedication of scientists and the fragile beauty of our planet. They remind us that every species, no matter how small, plays a role in the web of life.
why_it_matters: Wetlands are disappearing rapidly, and species like damselflies are an early warning system: when they vanish, it often signals water pollution or climate stress that will eventually affect human communities too. The contest makes that invisible connection visible.

background_read: Odisha, a state on India's eastern coast, is home to freshwater wetlands—shallow, waterlogged habitats that may look like ordinary ponds but support dragonflies, frogs, waterbirds, and fish.

Wetlands act like natural sponges and water filters: they absorb floodwater, trap pollutants, and store carbon, yet they are being drained and filled for farms, cities, and industry faster than most other ecosystems.
The image contest is run by BMC Ecology and Evolution and BMC Zoology, two scientific journals that publish peer-reviewed research on animals, plants, ecosystems, and evolutionary biology.
Damselflies are close relatives of dragonflies; one common difference is that many damselflies fold their wings over their backs when resting, while dragonflies usually hold them out to the sides.

Researchers use creatures like damselflies, frogs, and sea turtles as bioindicators—species whose presence or absence can reveal whether a habitat is healthy or stressed by pollution and climate change.
The Everglades, mentioned in the contest entries, is a vast subtropical wetland in Florida where undergraduate researchers monitor similar fragile ecosystems.

perspectives.description: Conservationists and science photographers see the contest as a powerful way to make overlooked species famous. A single vivid image can generate public curiosity about wetlands and the small creatures that keep them healthy. The prize also highlights the researchers who spend long hours studying fragile habitats.

Some ecologists caution that an award-winning photo can oversimplify complex problems. Attention may boost appreciation for one species without producing legal protections, funding, or habitat restoration. Wetland loss continues in many places even as images of their beauty circulate widely.

Scientists view damselflies and other contest subjects as bioindicators. Because these animals depend on both aquatic and terrestrial habitats, their presence or absence can reveal ecosystem health more reliably than a single measurement. The photos are therefore both art and ecological data.

The competition's impact could grow if it encourages wetland restoration and community-based monitoring. Mobile photography and citizen science may let more people document local species and habitat changes. The next step is turning that awareness into stronger policies that protect threatened wetlands before they disappear.
